blocks.content: A Role defines a namespace-scoped set of permissions, exactly what actions are allowed on which resources, but a Role by itself grants absolutely nothing until it is bound to someone.
A Role lives within, and only applies to, one specific namespace, defining a set of allowed actions purely for resources within that namespace.

blocks.alt: Permissions that apply within one namespace, and nowhere beyond it

blocks.content:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  namespace: default
  name: pod-reader
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

  namespace: default

rules:

blocks.content: A Role's rules are expressed as verbs (get, list, watch, create, update, delete) applied to specific resource types, a precise, granular vocabulary for describing exactly what is and is not allowed.

blocks.alt: A precise vocabulary of actions, applied to specific resource types

blocks.content: A Role granting only get, list, and watch on Pods within one namespace expresses exactly "read-only visibility into this namespace's Pods," nothing more, no ability to create, modify, or delete anything.

blocks.alt: A precisely scoped read-only grant, nothing broader than what is actually needed

blocks.content: This is genuinely important to understand: creating a Role by itself does not grant anyone anything at all, it is purely a definition of permissions, waiting to be connected to an actual subject, exactly the job of a RoleBinding, covered in the next topic.

blocks.alt: A definition sitting inert, until something actually binds it to a subject

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A Role defines a namespace-scoped set of permissions using verbs applied to specific resource types, a precise, granular vocabulary for access.
A Role alone grants nothing at all, it has to be connected to an actual user, group, or ServiceAccount, the job RoleBinding does, covered in the next topic.
